ask: Why is it on the path?
cards: A frontier beylik in Anatolia grew, with Janissary infantry, gunpowder artillery and a sophisticated bureaucracy, into a power spanning three continents for six centuries.
Osman I, a Turkoman chieftain of the Kayı clan, held a beylik in Bithynia on the Byzantine frontier, and his victory at Bapheus in 1301 gave the dynasty its military credibility.
In 1453 Mehmed II took the Byzantine capital after a siege in which heavy artillery played a major role, ending the Byzantine Empire and making the city the Ottoman capital.
Selim I defeated the Safavids at Chaldiran in 1514 and conquered the Mamluk Sultanate in 1516–1517, bringing Syria, Egypt and the holy cities of Arabia under Ottoman rule.
Suleiman, known in Turkish as Kanuni, the Lawgiver, conquered Belgrade, won at Mohács and besieged Vienna, in a reign treated as the height of Ottoman power and legal codification.
First recruited from Christian boys through the devshirme, the elite infantry became one of Europe's first standing armies to use firearms on a large scale, until their abolition in 1826.
From the Edict of Gülhane in 1839 to the constitution of 1876, Ottoman statesmen rebuilt the ministries, courts, schools, law codes and army and promised equality to all subjects.
Their Committee of Union and Progress forced the sultan to restore the constitution in 1908, later ruled as a dictatorship and masterminded the genocides of Ottoman Christians.
After the Ottoman defeat and the Allied occupation of Istanbul, Mustafa Kemal, an Ottoman army officer, led the Turkish national movement against the post-war partition of Anatolia.
Proclaimed in Ankara on 29 October 1923 after the Treaty of Lausanne, the Republic was turned by Mustafa Kemal's reforms into a secular nation state with a new civil code and alphabet.
